options.headline: AI THAT GETS PEOPLE TO CARE SOONER
options.text: Look at what the stories below have in common: reaching people in time. In Tanzania, people with diabetes were nearly twice as likely to get to an eye specialist. In New Jersey, AI alerts sent rapid response teams to patients at risk earlier, and deaths fell. In Wuhan, lung biopsies became safer. And a man with ALS got his words back. In each case, people stayed in charge, and AI helped them act sooner.

options.headline: CARE THAT REACHES PEOPLE
options.text: Purpose in health care is simple: get the right care to the right person in time. This edition shows AI helping with exactly that. An on-the-spot eye screening result that gets people to a specialist. An alert that brings a rapid response team to a bedside. A safer path for a biopsy needle. A brain implant that lets a man with ALS keep working and talking to his family.

options.headline: WHAT IF THE HELP CAME SOONER?
options.text: What changes when help arrives earlier? In Tanzania, an instant AI eye screening result nearly doubled the number of people who reached specialist care. At 11 New Jersey hospitals, earlier alerts came with fewer deaths among high-risk patients. Here are four stories, each with real numbers, of AI helping people get care sooner and more safely.

options.headline: SOONER, SAFER, HEARD
options.text: Four stories, four measured results: more people with diabetes reaching eye care in Tanzania, fewer deaths among high-risk patients in New Jersey, safer lung biopsies in Wuhan, and a man with ALS communicating nearly 2 million words from home. AI helping, people in charge.

options.headline: LESS FEAR, MORE FOLLOW-UP
options.text: The loudest AI stories are about what might go wrong. The quieter ones are about what is already going right, and they come with data. Two randomised trials, a study across 11 hospitals and nearly two years of daily home use: AI helping people reach eye care, survive a hospital stay, get a safer biopsy and speak again.

stories.institution: RWJBarnabas Health / Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School, Epic Deterioration Index rapid response
stories.teaser: AI alerts cut deaths among high-risk patients at 11 hospitals
stories.headline: AI early warnings cut deaths among high-risk patients from 23.1% to 18.6%
stories.why: Before-and-after study of 23,132 high-risk patients at 11 hospitals, NEJM AI
stories.bullet: Deaths fell from 23.1% to 18.6% for high-risk patients, with AI alerts
texts:
At 11 RWJBarnabas Health hospitals in New Jersey, an AI tool checks each patient's health record every 15 minutes and alerts the rapid response team when someone is at highest risk of a sudden decline.

Among 23,132 high-risk patients, deaths fell from 23.1% to 18.6% after it was introduced. The study is in NEJM AI.

#AIforGood

When a hospital patient starts to decline, every minute counts. RWJBarnabas Health and Rutgers paired an AI early-warning score with rapid response teams across 11 hospitals.

Rapid response visits for high-risk patients rose from 25.3% of stays to 37.5%, without a jump in ICU transfers. Deaths among those patients fell from 23.1% to 18.6%.

#AIforGood

What if the care team came before the crisis? At 11 New Jersey hospitals, AI alerts sent rapid response teams to the patients most at risk of sudden decline.

The risk-adjusted odds of dying in hospital fell by 18%. As one of the study's leaders put it, the benefit came from "the partnership around the algorithm."

#AIforGood
stories.og_title: RWJBarnabas Health and Rutgers Researchers Find AI Tool Helps Detect Patients at Risk Earlier

stories.institution: UC Davis Health BrainGate2 speech BCI, with Brown University and Mass General Brigham
stories.teaser: A man with ALS talks and works at home through a brain implant
stories.headline: Brain implant let a man with ALS communicate nearly 2 million words at home
stories.why: BrainGate2 clinical trial, one participant over nearly two years, Nature Medicine
stories.bullet: Nearly 2 million words at home, for a man with ALS using a brain implant
texts:
Casey Harrell lives with severe paralysis from ALS. Through a brain-computer interface from UC Davis Health, he has used his home computer for more than 3,800 hours over nearly two years.

He communicated close to 2 million words at an average of 56 words per minute, and rated 92% of his sentences accurate or mostly correct.

#AIforGood

For years, brain-computer interfaces lived in research labs. Casey Harrell, a man with ALS in the BrainGate2 trial, now uses one at home on a near-daily basis, without researcher support.

He sends emails and messages, browses the internet, stays in touch with family and keeps working, sometimes for more than 12 hours straight. The results are in Nature Medicine.

#AIforGood

What would you say if you got your voice back? Casey Harrell, who has ALS, has communicated 183,000 sentences through a brain implant from UC Davis Health, with over 99% word accuracy in controlled testing.

In his words, it lets him communicate "more in my natural way" than any other technology he has tried.

#AIforGood
stories.og_title: Brain-computer interface enables independent, accurate communication for man living with ALS

stories.institution: Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College (Huazhong University of Science and Technology), GPS-Lung navigation system
stories.teaser: AI guidance makes lung biopsies safer, with fewer collapsed lungs
stories.headline: AI navigation nearly halved collapsed lungs during lung biopsies in a trial
stories.why: Randomized trial of 220 patients at Wuhan Union Hospital sites, npj Digital Medicine
stories.bullet: Collapsed lungs nearly halved, from 23.9% to 12.7%, with AI-guided biopsies
texts:
Doctors at Union Hospital in Wuhan tested GPS-Lung, a generative AI navigation system for CT-guided lung nodule biopsies, in a randomized trial.

With the AI, a collapsed lung (pneumothorax) happened in 12.7% of procedures, against 23.9% with standard guidance. Procedures were shorter and needed fewer needle punctures. The results are in npj Digital Medicine.

#AIforGood

A lung biopsy is often the only way to know whether a nodule is cancer, but each extra needle pass adds risk. In a randomized trial in Wuhan, an AI navigation system cut punctures from 2.5 to 2.0 on average.

Operations took about three minutes less, radiation exposure fell, and collapsed lungs nearly halved.

#AIforGood

What if a biopsy needle found its target on the first try more often? Doctors at Union Hospital in Wuhan compared AI-guided lung biopsies with standard CT guidance in 220 patients.

With the AI, the rate of collapsed lungs fell from 23.9% to 12.7%, with less radiation and shorter procedures.

#AIforGood
stories.og_title: A Generative AI-powered navigation system for precision CBCT-guided lung biopsies: a randomized controlled trial

stories.institution: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine / Kilimanjaro Christian Medical Centre, AI diabetic eye screening (Tanzania)
stories.teaser: On-the-spot AI eye results nearly doubled follow-up care in Tanzania
stories.headline: AI eye screening nearly doubled specialist follow-up for people with diabetes
stories.why: Randomised trial of 2,378 people at 24 hospitals in Tanzania, The Lancet Global Health
stories.bullet: Nearly twice as many reached eye care, 35.9% vs 18.2%, with AI screening
texts:
In northern Tanzania, people with diabetes screened for eye disease usually waited weeks for a result by phone. In a randomised trial at 24 hospitals, AI gave the result on the spot, with face-to-face counselling.

Among those who needed specialist care, 35.9% reached the eye clinic within eight weeks, against 18.2% with standard screening.

#AIforGood

Diabetic eye disease can be treated, but only if people get to a specialist. A trial led by the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine and Kilimanjaro Christian Medical Centre tested AI screening with an instant result.

People who needed referral were nearly twice as likely to attend the eye clinic within eight weeks. The results are in The Lancet Global Health.

#AIforGood

What changes when a screening result comes on the spot instead of weeks later? In a trial of 2,378 people with diabetes in Tanzania, on-the-spot AI results and a conversation with a health worker before leaving made the difference.

Follow-up at the specialist eye clinic rose from 18.2% to 35.9%.

#AIforGood
stories.og_title: Artificial intelligence-supported diabetic retinopathy screening in Tanzania: a randomised controlled trial
